newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam to consider scrapping U.S. tourism venture.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam to consider scrapping U.S. tourism venture.

text.p: Vietnam's Ministry of Planning and Investment said on Monday it could withdraw the licence for a major beach resort project because the U.S. partner had failed to make an initial deposit of $2 million on time.

"There is no time left to transfer the $2 million," a ministry official said, noting that Maryland-based BBI Investment Group had been given until the end of November to transfer funds into the venture's bank account.
Officials at BBI's Hanoi office were not available to comment.
The project, a $243 million beach resort near the coastal city of Danang, has been in doubt for several months because it was alleged BBI had put no more than $200,000 into the account.
Robert Bernstein, president of the investment group, told reporters in Hanoi last May that talks with the ministry had cleared up problems threatening the project.

Describing the matter as a misunderstanding and oversight, he said that instead of making a deposit at the joint venture's bank, BBI had spent more than the required $2 million on costs directly associated with the project.

But problems lingered on and in November the ministry issued an ultimatum to BBI -- pay the deposit, secure a loan for the whole project and submit a new plan for its implementation by the end of the month or face the possibility of a licence withdrawal.

The daily Vietnam News on Saturday quoted a senior Vietnamese official involved in the project as saying that at least three other foreign investors were willing to step in if BBI failed to meet its deadline.
"If BBI...fails to meet the deadline all its hard work in surveys and feasibility studies over the last three years would become a windfall for others to pick up," the official said.

The report said interested parties included a venture between Japanese, Canadian and Italian interests called Transiting Commerce Technology, Asia Invest of France and an American firm which is already building a tourist complex just south of the planned BBI resort. It did not name the U.S. company.
